metadata.title: A long road to educational equity: Tracking trends through PISA 2000–2018
metadata.venue: International Journal of Educational Research Open

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study is a secondary, country-level analysis that aggregates equity indicator values (R-squared) published in official PISA reports across waves from 2000 to 2018. Because the analysis uses OECD-published summary statistics rather than student-level PISA microdata, standard PISA sampling weights (e.g., student weights) and replicate weights are not applicable in the way they would be for microdata-based estimation. The authors therefore do not report the use of complex survey design weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation procedures. The main preprocessing step is harmonizing the extracted R-squared indicators across subjects and waves (including using the 2006 report to retrieve earlier-wave indicators and excluding the 2009 wave due to missing subject coverage).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are generated for cognitive achievement scales in PISA microdata, but this paper does not model student-level achievement PVs. Instead, it uses OECD-published country-level equity indicators (R-squared values) extracted from official PISA reports and then fits simple linear trends over time at the country level. Missing-data handling is therefore not described in terms of PV imputation or student-level missingness procedures, because the dataset is constructed from published indicators rather than raw microdata.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study is based on secondary extraction of country-level equity indicators (R-squared of ESCS explaining PISA scores) from official PISA reports. It collects data for 87 countries that appear in PISA reports, but only 71 countries have at least two observation points (waves) to track dynamic change; only 30 countries have a complete set of observations spanning all six PISA waves. The analysis uses waves from 2000 to 2018 and excludes the 2009 wave because it only featured data for reading, which would break subject consistency. For waves 2000 and 2003, the authors use the 2006 report to retrieve the required indicators retrospectively. For each country, four equity indicators are constructed from report values: R-squared in Reading, Mathematics, Science, and an average across the three subjects; the trend analysis is then run using the available subject-average indicator per country.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This paper conducts a secondary, country-level trend analysis of socioeconomic equity in education using PISA 2000–2018. The authors extract OECD-published R-squared indicators (the share of variance in PISA scores explained by ESCS) for Reading, Mathematics, and Science for each participating country, then compute an average R-squared across subjects as the main equity indicator. They fit simple linear regressions per country to estimate the direction and magnitude of equity change over time (year coded from 2000 onward), and they report standard errors and statistical significance when at least three observations are available. Across 87 countries (with 71 having at least two waves), more countries show positive equity trends than negative, but most trends are not statistically robust due to limited observations and periodic fluctuations. The study finds that the OECD average R-squared decreased from 15% to 12.8% between 2000 and 2018, while equity improvements are concentrated in a subset of countries (e.g., Malaysia shows a significant negative trend; several OECD and partner countries show significant positive trends). Limitations include reliance on a single equity indicator (R-squared), potential comparability issues across PISA waves, and the absence of student-level modeling (so no PV-based estimation or ML prediction performance is evaluated). data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ML and PV/missing-data handling because the paper is not an empirical ML prediction study. It uses OECD-published, country-level equity indicators (R-squared values) and applies simple linear regression to estimate trends over time, without training machine learning models or using PISA microdata PVs. As a result, fields such as ml_techniques, main_findings (ML target/predictor performance), and student-level weighting are not applicable in the schema sense, and missing-data handling is not documented as it would be for microdata-based PV estimation.
